Our mission is to make lunar exploration more accessible by transforming NASA terrain data and orbital calculations into an immersive scientific experience. Visitors explore a 3D Moon, examine lunar south-pole landing sites, and visualize how terrain affects sunlight and direct-to-Earth communications.

Using NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data and JPL SPICE calculations, we analyzed Connecting Ridge and Mons Mouton across 169 hourly observations, revealing important differences in solar visibility and Earth communication opportunities.

The platform combines a seven-chapter guided mission, interactive terrain, scientific comparisons, evidence, and downloadable research. It also introduces a proposed six-point lunar infrastructure network and experimental quantum optimization research.

Lunar First Light explores how science, energy, communications, and future infrastructure can support humanity's next steps on the Moon.
details:
Lunar First Light — Seven Servers

Project Overview

Lunar First Light is an interactive lunar exploration, landing site navigation, and scientific research platform developed by Seven Servers for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Lunar Landing Site Navigator.

Seven Servers is a Detroit father-and-son space technology team founded by Preston Eaton and Preston Jordan Jr., with a long-term mission to develop infrastructure supporting peaceful, sustainable, and interconnected civilization across Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Lunar First Light represents an early demonstration of that mission.

Our project combines NASA lunar terrain data, orbital calculations, interactive three-dimensional visualization, and scientific research to investigate how future lunar operations could select locations, access solar energy, maintain communications with Earth, and eventually support interconnected infrastructure.

Our broader vision includes the Star of David, a proposed six-point satellite and energy infrastructure concept conceived by Preston Jordan Jr. The concept explores how solar-rich lunar regions, satellite-supported energy systems, and wireless power transmission could contribute to sustainable infrastructure on the Moon and potentially Earth.

We envision a future in which exploration is supported by reliable energy, communications, security, transportation, habitation, and resource systems. Lunar First Light investigates some of the scientific conditions necessary to begin pursuing that future.

The Challenge

The Moon's south pole presents significant opportunities and engineering challenges for future exploration.

Lunar polar regions experience unusual illumination conditions. Mountains, ridges, craters, and surrounding terrain can obstruct sunlight or direct visibility of Earth.

These conditions matter when considering where to establish solar-powered infrastructure, maintain Earth communications, operate robotic systems, and eventually support larger lunar facilities.

NASA's Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge calls for an intuitive application that allows mission planners, researchers, educators, and the public to compare candidate landing sites and observation dates while visualizing the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon.

Seven Servers approached this challenge by asking:

How can scientific information about lunar terrain, solar availability, and Earth communications help determine where humanity could establish future energy and infrastructure systems on the Moon?

This question also connects to our longer-term interest in orbital energy collection, satellite networks, and sustainable infrastructure linking Earth and the Moon.

Our Solution

Lunar First Light transforms NASA scientific information into an interactive exploration and research experience.

The application brings lunar geography, scientific measurements, visualizations, and research findings together within one platform.

Its features include:

  • An interactive 3D Moon with navigable lunar terrain.
  • A narrated seven-chapter guided mission.
  • Lunar south-pole exploration and site visualization.
  • A 169-hour scientific observation timeline.
  • Sun and Earth visibility comparisons.
  • Terrain-horizon analysis for selected lunar locations.
  • Scientific evidence and downloadable research findings.
  • Interactive energy, communications, mobility, and infrastructure concepts.
  • Visualization of a proposed six-point lunar infrastructure network.
  • Research concepts associated with the Star of David satellite architecture.
  • Experimental quantum optimization research.

The application is organized into four primary sections.

Mission: An immersive three-dimensional environment where visitors explore the Moon, navigate between lunar locations, follow the guided mission, and examine changing conditions.

Analysis: Scientific research comparing candidate lunar south-pole sites, including sunlight and Earth visibility calculations.

Systems & Research: An interactive environment exploring proposed lunar infrastructure, energy systems, communications, mobility, satellite-supported concepts, and computational research.

Report: Published scientific findings, supporting evidence, methodology, source information, and downloadable research results.

Scientific Methodology

Our research incorporates NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LRO/LOLA) terrain elevation data, NAIF SPICE, and JPL orbital ephemerides.

We evaluated two candidate lunar south-pole locations:

Connecting Ridge and Mons Mouton.

The scientific observation period covers November 1 through November 8, 2026, using 169 hourly observations.

Our analysis uses lunar digital elevation models to estimate the local terrain horizon surrounding each location.

We then calculate the modeled positions of the Sun and Earth relative to those horizons to evaluate geometric visibility at each observation time.

The research uses high-resolution local terrain data for Connecting Ridge and regional terrain coverage for Mons Mouton.

This approach allows us to investigate how different geographical conditions influence potential sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

The current calculations evaluate modeled geometric visibility rather than directly measuring electrical generation, communications link performance, or landing safety.

Scientific Findings

Our published analysis identified significant differences between the two locations during the selected observation period.

Connecting Ridge

  • Modeled Sun-center visibility: 169 of 169 hourly observations.
  • Modeled Earth-center visibility: 55 of 169 hourly observations.

Mons Mouton

  • Modeled Sun-center visibility: 0 of 169 hourly observations.
  • Modeled Earth-center visibility: 64 of 169 hourly observations.

During this observation window, Connecting Ridge demonstrated continuous modeled Sun-center visibility, while Mons Mouton showed no Sun-center visibility above its modeled terrain horizon.

Earth visibility presented a different pattern, with Mons Mouton showing more observations with the Earth center visible than Connecting Ridge.

These findings illustrate an important consideration for future lunar infrastructure: a location presenting favorable solar conditions may have different direct-to-Earth communication opportunities than another candidate site.

Our research demonstrates why terrain, illumination, observation timing, and communications geometry should be evaluated together.

The results provide a scientific starting point for investigating where future solar-energy facilities, communications stations, and supporting infrastructure might be located.

Earth Communications and Interconnected Infrastructure

Earth-space communications are a central component of the Seven Servers mission.

As humanity expands its activities beyond Earth, communications infrastructure will be essential for coordinating scientific research, robotics, energy systems, transportation, resource operations, and eventually human settlements.

Lunar First Light investigates one foundational component of that challenge: determining when Earth is geometrically visible from a particular lunar location.

These visibility windows can help inform future research into direct-to-Earth communications, satellite relays, and interconnected lunar operations.

Our broader vision includes reliable satellite networks, secure information exchange, resilient communications architecture, and technologies capable of connecting operations across Earth, the Moon, and eventually Mars.

The Star of David concept contributes to this larger vision by exploring how a coordinated satellite architecture might support energy and communications infrastructure.

Lunar First Light begins with measurable lunar geography and orbital conditions that can inform future engineering research into these systems.

Star of David — Proposed Satellite and Solar Energy Infrastructure

One of the central concepts behind Seven Servers' long-term infrastructure vision is the Star of David satellite system, proposed by Preston Jordan Jr.

The Star of David is envisioned as a six-point satellite and infrastructure architecture exploring solar-energy collection, transmission, and interconnected operations between the Moon, satellites, and Earth.

The concept begins with the identification of lunar regions that experience extended periods of sunlight.

Certain lunar polar locations have been investigated for their unusually favorable illumination conditions. Our concept considers locations with approximately 97% sunlight availability as potential targets for further scientific evaluation.

The proposed system explores several interconnected elements.

1. Solar-Rich Lunar Locations

Use lunar terrain and illumination research to identify locations where sustained solar exposure could support energy collection and future surface infrastructure.

Lunar First Light begins this process through terrain-horizon analysis and modeled Sun visibility.

2. Six-Point Satellite Architecture

Explore a proposed configuration of interconnected satellite or infrastructure nodes organized around the Star of David concept.

These nodes could be studied for possible energy collection, coordination, communications, or supporting infrastructure roles.

3. Solar Energy Collection

Investigate how solar collection systems placed in favorable lunar or orbital environments might contribute to future energy infrastructure.

4. Wireless Energy Transmission

Explore the feasibility of transmitting collected solar energy through future wireless power transmission technologies to receiving systems on the lunar surface and potentially Earth.

This would require additional research into orbital geometry, beam transmission, receiving infrastructure, conversion efficiency, pointing accuracy, and operational safety.

5. Earth-Moon Communications

Examine how satellite-supported communications and coordination systems could help connect lunar facilities with Earth-based infrastructure.

6. Sustainable Expansion

Investigate how energy collection, communications, and surface infrastructure could eventually support larger lunar operations, resource systems, habitats, and future transportation networks.

The Star of David is a proposed engineering concept rather than a deployed satellite system.

Lunar First Light currently demonstrates relevant foundational research through lunar terrain analysis, geometric Sun and Earth visibility calculations, scientific comparisons, and conceptual infrastructure visualization.

The proposed satellite geometry, power-transmission mechanisms, energy delivery to Earth, and operational performance remain subjects for future engineering validation.

The concept reflects our interest in advancing from scientific observations toward interconnected infrastructure systems capable of supporting peaceful, sustainable development across Earth and space.

Proposed Six-Point Lunar Surface Network

Alongside the Star of David satellite concept, Seven Servers explores a proposed six-point lunar surface infrastructure network.

This research concept considers how multiple lunar locations and supporting facilities could operate together instead of functioning as isolated installations.

Potential systems include:

  • Solar energy generation and distribution.
  • Communications stations and relay infrastructure.
  • Surface mobility and robotic operations.
  • Resource collection and processing.
  • Supporting facilities and operational coordination.
  • Future expansion into larger lunar infrastructure networks.

The proposed surface network and Star of David satellite concept represent related areas of our long-term infrastructure research.

By combining terrain analysis, communications visibility, and conceptual system layouts, Lunar First Light provides an initial environment for exploring how future energy and infrastructure planning could be informed by scientific observations.

Quantum Computing Research

We incorporated Microsoft's Quantum Development Kit into an experimental six-node optimization study.

The research evaluates 64 possible binary node configurations through classical computation and a six-qubit quantum software simulation using a QAOA-like approach.

This experiment explores how different computational methods could eventually contribute to infrastructure planning and optimization.

The current study is a software simulation rather than an execution on quantum hardware.

Its purpose is to investigate computational approaches that may have future applications in multi-node energy and infrastructure coordination.

Technology and AI-Assisted Development

Lunar First Light combines web development, scientific computing, three-dimensional visualization, and experimental optimization research.

Technologies used include:

  • Next.js, React, and TypeScript for the web application.
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber for interactive 3D visualization.
  • Python and FastAPI for scientific computation and application services.
  • NASA LRO/LOLA digital elevation data for lunar terrain analysis.
  • NAIF SPICE and JPL ephemerides for orbital calculations.
  • Microsoft Quantum Development Kit for quantum simulation research.
  • Automated testing and research reporting tools.

We also used OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini through Antigravity to assist with application development, interface design, debugging, scientific explanations, and documentation.

The platform combines scientific calculations with immersive visualization to make complex lunar conditions easier to explore and compare.

The published research results are supported by the project's documented computational methods and source datasets.

Creativity and Innovation

Lunar First Light brings together several scientific and technological disciplines within one interactive environment.

The platform combines lunar terrain visualization, orbital geometry, scientific comparisons, guided exploration, Earth communications analysis, infrastructure concepts, and quantum computing research.

Our approach connects immediate scientific questions about lunar locations with larger questions about the infrastructure future operations may require.

The project also reflects a father-and-son collaboration focused on translating a long-term technological vision into practical research and working software.

The Star of David extends this vision into the exploration of coordinated satellite systems and future solar-energy transmission between the Moon and Earth.

Rather than examining lunar locations as isolated points on a map, Seven Servers is exploring how their environmental conditions could influence interconnected energy, communications, and surface infrastructure.

Mission and Long-Term Impact

The mission of Seven Servers is to help develop the technological infrastructure for peaceful, sustainable, and interconnected civilization across Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Our vision extends beyond a single lunar landing site or research application.

We envision a future in which scientific discovery, advanced computing, reliable communications, sustainable energy, secure information systems, and responsible infrastructure development work together to support human progress beyond Earth.

That vision includes artificial intelligence, satellite networks, Earth-space communications, blockchain-based verification, quantum-resistant cybersecurity, robotics, sustainable habitats, food production, and resource systems.

We are particularly interested in how these technologies can support one another.

Reliable energy systems can support communications and scientific operations. Communications networks can connect remote facilities and people across vast distances. Secure digital infrastructure can help protect the integrity of operational records and information.

Sustainable habitats, food systems, transportation, and resource infrastructure can eventually support longer-term human presence.

The proposed Star of David satellite system reflects our ambition to investigate how favorable solar conditions and future energy-transmission technologies might contribute to sustainable energy systems serving lunar infrastructure and potentially Earth.

Our humanitarian vision is equally important.

Seven Servers seeks to contribute to a future where technological advancement supports peaceful cooperation, human well-being, scientific collaboration, and sustainable development.

Lunar First Light represents an early research step toward that larger objective.

By investigating lunar terrain, sunlight visibility, direct-to-Earth communications opportunities, and proposed interconnected infrastructure, we are beginning to examine the conditions future lunar operations must address.

The platform can also serve researchers, educators, students, and mission planners by making scientific data more accessible and providing an environment for exploring lunar geography and infrastructure questions.

For Seven Servers, the Moon is one stage in a larger mission connecting Earth, lunar infrastructure, satellite-supported systems, and future operations on Mars.

Our long-term ambition is to contribute to technologies that allow humanity to live, communicate, collaborate, and build peacefully across those environments.
